passage:
The shouting started again after dinner: Papa and Chacha arguing about the shop, loud enough to rattle the steel glasses. Sharmila, eleven, felt her fists go tight. She wanted to throw something. Usually she ran laps around the colony ground when this happened, but tonight it was pouring. So she tied her laces and ran the building stairs instead: ground floor to fifth, fifth to ground, again and again.
Her cousin Minakshi found her on the fourth round, red-faced and panting. "Want company?" They ran together until Sharmila's legs shook and the anger felt smaller than the stairs.
Upstairs, the voices had gone quiet. Sharmila drank two glasses of water and felt calm enough to sleep.

qa.q: Where did Sharmila run when it was pouring?
qa.a: The building stairs, ground floor to fifth and back again.

qa.q: What was Sharmila feeling when her fists went tight?
qa.a: Furious and helpless about the shouting between Papa and Chacha, with an urge to throw something.

qa.q: What choice did Sharmila make when the rain blocked her usual laps, and why did it work?
qa.a: She ran the stairs instead, putting the anger into hard, safe effort until it felt smaller, rather than throwing something.

qa.q: What might Minakshi have understood on finding Sharmila on the stairs?
qa.a: Minakshi probably guessed the shouting had upset Sharmila and chose to run alongside rather than ask questions, so Sharmila felt less alone.

grounding: An eleven-year-old furious about a family quarrel runs the building stairs in the rain until the anger passes.

passage:
When Amma and Appa started arguing about money again in their Chennai flat, Sangeeta, nine, didn't slam her door. She went to the corner of the balcony where her practice pad and drumsticks lived, the ones from her Saturday class at the music school. Tak-tak-tak. Faster. Harder. She played the rhythm her teacher had taught her, then made up a louder one.
Her elder sister Gopika leaned in the doorway. "Angry beat?" Sangeeta nodded without stopping.
Fifteen minutes later her arms were tired and her breathing had slowed. The argument inside had turned into a low murmur. Sangeeta put down the sticks, went in, and asked Appa to check her maths homework.

qa.q: Where did Sangeeta keep her practice pad and drumsticks?
qa.a: In the corner of the balcony.

qa.q: Why did playing faster and harder help Sangeeta?
qa.a: She was angry and upset about the argument, and drumming gave that energy somewhere safe and skilful to go until her body calmed.

qa.q: Which choice of Gopika's helped, and why?
qa.a: Asking 'Angry beat?' and letting her keep playing, which named the feeling without stopping the drumming that was calming her.

qa.q: How might Amma and Appa feel if they noticed the angry beat from the balcony?
qa.a: They might realise their argument was upsetting Sangeeta and feel sorry, perhaps choosing to talk more quietly or away from the children.

grounding: A nine-year-old angry about her parents' argument drums on her practice pad until the storm passes, then rejoins the family.

passage:
"Lavanya, where are you going?"
"Out."
"Your father and I weren't shouting at you, kanna."
"You were shouting. Everyone heard." The door banged.
Ten minutes later, Sarika found her daughter in the courtyard with her skipping rope, counting under her breath. "Ninety-eight, ninety-nine, hundred."
"Can I sit here?"
"If you don't talk about it." Swish, swish. "Hundred and fifty."
"Okay."
Swish, swish. "Two hundred." Lavanya stopped, panting, hands on her knees. "I hate it when you two fight."
"I know. I'm sorry you heard it."
"Amma, can you count for me? I want to reach three hundred."
"Go on. I'll count."
"Two hundred and one..."

qa.q: How many skips was Lavanya aiming for?
qa.a: Three hundred.

qa.q: Why did Lavanya want her mother not to talk about it while she skipped?
qa.a: She was still too angry and hurt about the fighting to talk, and counting skips helped her burn the feeling off first.

qa.q: What choice of Sarika's helped the anger pass?
qa.a: Sitting nearby without lecturing, apologising simply, and then counting the skips, which supported Lavanya's own way of calming down.

qa.q: What might Sarika be feeling as she counts for Lavanya?
qa.a: Probably guilty that the shouting was heard, and relieved to be let back in; counting is a small way to make amends.

grounding: A girl upset by her parents' quarrel skips rope in the courtyard until the anger eases, while her mother sits and counts with her.

passage:
I'm Ishita, and last winter I learned something about being angry. Papa and Dada kept fighting about selling the old house in the village. They shouted so loud the neighbours' dog barked. I hated it. My whole body felt hot and fizzy, and once I nearly threw my water bottle at the wall.
Instead I took my football down to the back wall of our building. Left foot, right foot, bang, bang, bang. I counted: fifty, a hundred. When I kicked hard, the ball came back hard, so I had to be quick and careful.
After a while the fizz went out of my arms and legs. I came back up tired and sweaty, and I could tell Mumma how I felt.
Now I can do two hundred passes without missing. Coach picked me for the under-eleven team.

qa.q: Where did Ishita take the football?
qa.a: Down to the back wall of the building.

qa.q: How did Ishita feel during Papa and Dada's fights, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Angry and upset; Ishita's whole body felt hot and fizzy, and once there was an urge to throw the water bottle at the wall.

qa.q: Which choice turned Ishita's anger into something useful?
qa.a: Taking the football to the wall instead of throwing the bottle; the kicking used up the fizz safely and built a real skill.

qa.q: How might Mumma see Ishita coming back tired and ready to talk?
qa.a: Mumma probably feels relieved that Ishita found a safe way through the anger, and glad they can talk about the fighting calmly.

grounding: Shows a child furious about a family quarrel kicking a football against a wall until the storm passes, turning the energy into a safe, skilled activity.

passage:
Community centre music room, teacher's note, Tarun
Nilesh, 11, came to dhol class on Thursday with his jaw clenched and his laces untied. At pickup last week his mother told me there's been a lot of shouting at home between his father and uncle over the family shop.
He didn't say hello. He picked up the sticks and hit the dhol so hard the whole room jumped. I didn't stop him. I only said, "Good power. Now put it inside the eight-beat." He did: loud, then louder, but on the beat.
After twenty minutes his shoulders came down. He played the new pattern twice without a mistake, grinned for the first time, and asked, "Can I stay for the next batch?"
Next: offer him a place in the Diwali performance; ask his mother how things are at home.

qa.q: What did Tarun say when Nilesh first hit the dhol?
qa.a: "Good power. Now put it inside the eight-beat."

qa.q: What does Nilesh hitting the dhol so hard suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he arrived full of anger from the shouting at home and needed somewhere big and safe to put it.

qa.q: Why was Tarun's choice not to stop him a good one?
qa.a: Letting Nilesh keep the power but asking for it on the beat turned the fury into a skill, and after twenty minutes his shoulders came down.

qa.q: What would change if Tarun had told Nilesh to stop banging?
qa.a: Nilesh might have felt scolded on top of the shouting at home and left with the anger still unspent, instead of calming down and grinning.

grounding: Illustrates, in a music teacher's note, a child angry about a family quarrel drumming until the storm passes, with the energy steered into rhythm and skill.
